title: Wherever he went (Mark 6:53–56)
hook: villages lay the sick in the marketplaces just to touch his fringe

segments.voice: Yesterday, a figure on the water before dawn, and three phrases: take heart. It is I. Don't be afraid. Who did you say take heart to? Day one hundred eighty-five.

The boat lands at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the lake's western shore. The moment Jesus steps out, someone recognizes him. And then it's like watching news spread before phones. People run through the whole region. Anyone with someone sick at home picks them up, mat and all, and carries them to wherever they've heard he is. Village, town, farm, it doesn't matter. Today is just four verses long. No big speech, no single story. A snapshot of what it was like. Today: wherever he went.

Here's the last verse, in the old King James Bible: "And whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets, and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment: and as many as touched him were made whole." The streets here are the marketplaces, the open squares at the heart of every town. Picture the busiest square you know, lined with people on mats, waiting. And what do they ask for? Not a speech. Not even a word. Just to touch the border of his garment. Remember the woman in the crowd, a week ago. What she did in secret, a whole region now does in the open. The border, in Greek, is kraspedon, a fringe or tassel. The law of Moses told the people of Israel to wear tassels on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue, to remember God's commandments. Many Jews still wear them today, called tzitzit. So the fringe they reached for was very likely one of those: Jesus dressed as an observant Jew, and the sick reaching for the reminder of God's commands on his clothes. And with that, the second part of Mark closes. Seeds, storms and loaves. The sower from a boat. Why parables. A lamp on a stand. Seed growing secretly. Asleep on a cushion. Legion. Go home and tell. The hem of his garment. Talitha koum. The carpenter at home. Travel light. John's head. Sheep without a shepherd. It is I. And now, wherever he went. Next, Mark asks the question straight out: who is this?
screen: `WHITHERSOEVER HE ENTERED.` · `THE SICK LAID IN THE STREETS.` · `KRASPEDON — A FRINGE, A TASSEL.` · `SEEDS, STORMS AND LOAVES: DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring someone's need into prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who carried their sick to the square. Now think of someone you'd carry if you could. Someone ill, worn out, in need of healing of any kind. Picture yourself setting their mat down in the square. If you pray, you can bring their need to God by name, the way the villages brought theirs. If you don't pray, hold them in mind, and ask who could help them that you could reach. The bell holds the time.
Wherever he went. Villages, towns and farms bringing their sick to the marketplace, just to touch the fringe of his cloak.
Your line: touch the fringe. Today, carry one person's need somewhere it can be met: to God, if you pray, or to someone who can help. Day one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians bring the needs of others into prayer by name, alone or aloud in church, and many congregations keep prayer lists for the sick of their community.

fork.setup: word spreads that Jesus has landed nearby. someone you love is too sick to walk. what do you do?
options: wait until he comes to your village.
carry them on a mat to wherever he is.
send a message asking him to visit.
fork.reveal: people carried their sick on mats to wherever they heard he was, and laid them in the streets to touch his fringe.

original.note: Greek: a border or tassel, the fringe on the corner of a garment.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hem is just the edge of his robe.
what it means: whole regions carried their sick to the marketplaces just to touch the fringe of his cloak.
what a scholar hears: kraspedon, likely the tassels the law of Moses commands on garments, the tzitzit many Jews still wear.

sources.quoted: And whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets, and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment: and as many as touched him were made whole.

notes: Last day of the part 'Mark 4–6 · Seeds, storms and loaves'; the teach names its days and points to 'Mark 7–9 · Who is this?'.
kraspedon as tzitzit (Numbers 15:38–39) is a common but not universal reading; stated as 'very likely'. Confirm.
